content: If Mycobacterium tuberculosis is resistant to isoniazid or rifampin but remains susceptible to ethionamide, ethionamide should be administered alongside at least one other drug to which the M. tuberculosis isolate is known to be susceptible. If the tuberculosis strain is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampin but remains susceptible to ethionamide, ethionamide should be combined with at least two other drugs to which the M. tuberculosis isolate is known to be susceptible. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is recommended for all patients undergoing tuberculosis treatment to ensure adherence and effectiveness. Baseline and periodic monitoring of liver function tests (LFTs), thyroid function tests (TFTs), and blood glucose levels are essential during ethionamide therapy. Ethionamide, when co-administered with cycloserine, may increase the toxicity of both drugs due to pharmacodynamic synergy, leading to enhanced central nervous system (CNS) toxicity and an increased risk of seizures. Caution and close monitoring are advised in such cases. Ethionamide can also increase isoniazid levels through an unspecified interaction mechanism, necessitating careful monitoring. Additionally, ethionamide may reduce the efficacy of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering their metabolism, and co-administration with antibiotics may further decrease their effectiveness by disrupting colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. Ethionamide is associated with a range of adverse effects, including gastrointestinal disturbances (e.g., nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), postural hypotension, depression, dizziness, drowsiness, headache, peripheral neuropathy, psychosis, photosensitivity, rash, excessive salivation, gynecomastia, hypoglycemia, impotence, anorexia, dyspepsia, metallic taste, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver transaminases, hepatitis, optic neuritis, visual changes, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). If signs or symptoms of SCARs develop, the suspected drug(s) should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Ethionamide should not be used as monotherapy for tuberculosis due to the rapid development of resistance. It must be combined with other drugs based on susceptibility testing results. Therapy may be initiated before susceptibility results are available if deemed appropriate by the physician. Ophthalmologic examinations, including fundoscopy, should be performed before and periodically during therapy to monitor for optic neuritis or visual changes. Excessive alcohol consumption should be avoided, as it may increase the risk of psychotic reactions and liver dysfunction. Ethionamide is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. It may be bacteriostatic or bactericidal depending on the concentration and the susceptibility of the organism. Pregnant women should avoid using ethionamide as its effects on labor and delivery are unknown, and it may harm the fetus. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and it is unclear if the drug passes into breast milk. Patients with diabetes, thyroid disease, hepatic impairment, or HIV (due to potential malabsorption syndrome) should use ethionamide with caution. Ethionamide may lower blood sugar levels, so diabetic patients should monitor their blood glucose regularly and report symptoms of hypoglycemia (e.g., sweating, shaking, rapid heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, tingling in hands/feet) to their doctor immediately. Ethionamide may interact with other medications, altering their effects or increasing the risk of serious side effects. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and share it with their healthcare provider. In case of overdose, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Routine laboratory tests, including sputum tests, liver/thyroid function tests, blood glucose levels, and complete blood counts, should be conducted during therapy. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Ethionamide should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Proper disposal of expired or unused medication is necessary. Always consult a healthcare professional for complete information about ethionamide and its use in your specific health condition.
